analysis.one_liner: Makes oil spillers strictly liable for cleanup costs and damages and creates a federal fund to pay spill victims.
analysis.headline: Two House committees reported this oil-spill liability bill in September 1989, but the House never voted on it; on November 9 the House was directed to companion bill H.R. 1465 for further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Written in the aftermath of the Exxon Valdez spill, this bill would have made the company responsible for an oil spill strictly liable — without needing to prove fault — for cleanup costs and for damages to property, natural resources, and local livelihoods. It would create an Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund to pay claims the spiller cannot or will not pay, require vessels and facilities to prove they can cover their liability before entering U.S. waters, and direct new prevention steps: response plans, equipment inspections, vessel traffic systems, tug-escort studies, and research. It also tightens license rules for merchant mariners with alcohol problems.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities and people whose livelihoods depend on clean water: the bill lets anyone who derives at least 25 percent of earnings from affected property or natural resources recover lost profits, and lets federal, state, and tribal trustees recover the cost of restoring damaged natural resources. Taxpayers benefit because the responsible party — not the public — bears cleanup costs first, with a federal fund as backstop.

how_it_helps.text: The party responsible for a spill is jointly, severally, and strictly liable for removal costs and damages, so victims do not have to prove negligence to be paid.

Recoverable damages include lost profits or impaired earning capacity for claimants who get at least a quarter of their earnings from the damaged property or natural resources — a category aimed at fishermen and small tourism businesses.

Damages to natural resources are recoverable by federal, state, and Indian tribe trustees, who must then restore, rehabilitate, or replace the damaged resources, and a civil penalty up to the greater of $1 million or half the party's liability applies when damage cannot be restored.

An Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund pays uncompensated claims for removal costs and damages, with a per-incident maximum of $1 billion, and any person paid compensation gains subrogation rights to recover from the responsible party.
Vessels over 300 gross tons and vessels lightering oil must prove financial responsibility; those that cannot certify it can be denied clearance, denied entry to U.S. ports, or detained.

The bill directs mandatory response plans, no-notice training drills, three-year equipment inspections and certification, regional response capability requirements for owners and operators, vessel traffic systems with mandatory participation and user fees, and studies of tug escorts, tanker free zones, and crew sizes.
The Coast Guard could refuse or revoke merchant seamen licenses for current or chronic alcohol abusers, and a vessel's chief mate must assume command if the captain appears intoxicated.

analysis.who_pays: Oil shippers, tanker owners, and facility operators bear strict liability, cleanup costs, civil penalties, financial-responsibility requirements, and response-equipment mandates; those costs are ultimately passed to consumers in the price of oil. The federal Fund — financed by oil-related receipts under the tax code — backstops claims above what the spiller pays.

drawbacks.text: Liability is capped: tankers at the greater of $500 per gross ton or $5 million but no more than $150 million, other vessels at the greater of $300 per ton or $500,000, and facilities at $75 million — so for a very large spill the public fund, capped at $1 billion per incident, pays costs above the cap.

The caps are lifted only for willful misconduct or gross negligence within the 'privity or knowledge' of the responsible party, or a safety-regulation violation in that same privity — a high bar for claimants to meet against a corporation.
Except for personal injury or wrongful death, the bill preempts other court actions over a discharge, channeling all claims into this federal regime and its procedures rather than state courts.

Much of Title II consists of studies and reports — on crew sizes, dredge modifications, tanker free zones, liners for storage tanks, and vessel-movement authority — rather than immediate mandates, so some protections depend on later action.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is a good one for the public: it shifts the first line of spill costs from taxpayers to the companies that move and store oil, and gives fishermen, coastal property owners, and resource trustees a clear right to compensation. The main honest caveat is the liability caps — a catastrophic spill could exceed them, leaving the public fund and ultimately taxpayers to cover the difference — and the fact that the caps are hard to pierce even in cases of serious corporate fault.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared subcommittees and two full House committees in amended form in August and September 1989, but instead of a floor vote the House was directed to companion bill H.R. 1465 for further action, and this bill's number died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 27, 1989, by Rep. Glenn Anderson and jointly referred to three committees; the Public Works and Transportation Committee held subcommittee markups and reported it amended on September 13, and the Science, Space and Technology Committee reported it amended on September 22.

On November 9, 1989, the House action history records 'For Further Action See H.R.1465' — the House pursued companion oil-spill legislation under a different bill number rather than voting on H.R. 3027 itself.
H.R. 3027 never received a floor vote and died at the end of the 101st Congress on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coastal communities, fishermen, and taxpayers were not left empty-handed, because the House kept the subject alive through H.R. 1465; oil shippers avoided this bill's strict-liability terms only under its own number, not permanently.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The liability regime lived on in H.R. 1465

for.name: Rep. Glenn M. Anderson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 27, 1989, joined by Reps. Hammerschmidt, Nowak, and Stangeland.

for.name: House Committee on Public Works and Transportation
for.what_they_did: Held subcommittee markups, forwarded the bill amended on September 12, and reported it on September 13, 1989 (H. Rept. 101-241, Part I).

for.name: House Committee on Science, Space and Technology
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill amended on September 22, 1989 (H. Rept. 101-241, Part II), adding the oil pollution research provisions.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a floor vote, so no recorded vote shows a partisan split; its six cosponsors split evenly, three Republicans and three Democrats.

industries.note: The bill makes them strictly liable for cleanup costs and damages, requires proof of financial responsibility before entering U.S. waters, and lets the government deny entry to vessels that cannot certify it. Costs above their liability caps fall on a public fund.

industries.industry: Oil producers and onshore/offshore facility operators
industries.note: They face strict liability, a $75 million facility liability cap, civil penalties up to $1 million for unrestoreable natural-resource damage, and mandatory response plans and equipment. The liability cap and the ability to self-insure partially soften the burden.

The financial-responsibility mandate lets responsible parties show compliance through insurance, surety bonds, guarantees, or letters of credit, creating a large new market for coverage. The mandate serves the public's interest in compensated spills.

industries.industry: Oil spill response and cleanup industry
industries.note: Mandatory regional response capability, no-notice drills, equipment certification every three years, and response plans create guaranteed demand for cleanup equipment and trained personnel.

The bill authorizes a coordinated federal research program, at least three regional research centers, grants to universities and research institutions, and appropriations from the Fund for fiscal years 1991-1995.
